The fourth pew on the right has a canvas bag on the end of it, at the aisle. When Jack gets there Lena lifts the bag into her lap and goes back to her worship aid, and he sits down where it was.

Across the aisle, in the fourth pew on the left, where she always is, Becca sits between Joey and Kenzie Rourke with her rosary in her hands. She doesn’t look over. Not at the entrance hymn, not at the readings.

The first reading is Maccabees again; it has been Maccabees all week, old men refusing things. Then Fr. Osei reads the Gospel, Luke, Jesus coming over the hill and seeing the city and weeping over it. *If this day you only knew what makes for peace — but now it is hidden from your eyes.*

“He is not angry here. Notice,” Osei says, from the step, without notes. “He comes over the hill and sees the city and he cries, the way a doctor cries in his car afterward, never in front of the family. They did not know the hour they were visited. Most of us find out later.” He looks out at the fifteen of them a moment. “Later is also an hour. God keeps those too.” Ninety seconds, and he sits down.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand.

s02.slug: THURSDAY · 1:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: On the Fishbowl TV, with the sound off, CNN is still running Kabul: Hamid Karzai in his karakul hat and his striped cloak, taking the oath again in a hall full of men applauding without any noise. The crawl underneath is about the UC Regents and a fee hike, and students outside a meeting at UCLA. Jack is on the couch under it with Hale’s prompt folded into the reader on his knee — WHETHER A PROMISE BINDS WHEN ITS REASON IS GONE; COSTIGAN: NO; eight pages, Monday at nine — and a notebook open beside it with the date at the top and nothing under the date. Every time the east stairwell door bangs he looks up. It’s never anybody: a kid with a bike helmet, two girls carrying a laundry basket by its handles, a boy in a Lakers jersey eating cereal out of a mug.
Laney comes through from the mailroom with a Diet Coke and stops behind the couch. She doesn’t move on. Eventually he has to look up.
“You look like a girl who lost Miss Teen Dallas to a baton twirler.”
“It’s Becca.”
“Sure it is.”
She puts the Diet Coke in his hand. It’s cold and open, one sip gone, her lip gloss on the rim, and she lets go of it and keeps walking.
At the door she stops. “I’ve been instructed to be nice to Becca. Effective today. I don’t know where to *put* it.”

Through the Fishbowl glass Theo is out on the Anacapa lawn in his sunglasses with his iPhone to his ear, looking in at Jack. When Jack looks back, Theo turns around and gives his attention to the sky, still talking.

The Hobart is mid-cycle with its door down, a long wet roar, and over it Rudy’s transistor has KNX out of Los Angeles — the Regents again, students chanting about thirty-two percent outside a building at UCLA — and under all of it the fryer and the ticket wheel. Jack has been at the sink twenty minutes. He has done a rack of coffee cups, and then the same rack again, because he wasn’t looking.

Gloria comes up behind him and unties his apron herself. He feels the knot go at the small of his back; then she lifts the strap off over his head, the way you’d take a bib off a kid, and folds it over her arm.
“Hon. Whatever it is, I don’t want it near my pie case.” She looks at him. “Is it the apple?”
“Yeah.”
“Mm,” says Gloria. She hangs the apron on its nail by the walk-in.
Rudy doesn’t turn around from the flat-top. “Go home, mijo.”
It’s six hours at eight dollars, plus a Thursday’s share of the tips, and Thursdays are never much. He gets his jacket off the hook. He lets it go.

On his way out past the register Gloria hands him a to-go box without a word and goes back to a fisherman’s refill. He doesn’t open it till he’s out on the planks under the wharf lights, with the sea lions arguing somewhere below the pilings. It’s a slice of the pecan.

s04.slug: THURSDAY · 8:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 → THE EAST STAIRS
body: Theo is dressing for midnight in front of the closet mirror, on Laney’s orders: a TEAM JACOB T-shirt, the iron-on kind from a mall kiosk, and over it a cashmere sweater the color of wet sand, tugged down carefully until not one letter shows.
“For deniability,” he says.

In the mirror he watches Jack sit on the end of his own bed with his boots still on. He says nothing about it. He says nothing about anything. On the desk the RAZR has nothing new on it; Jack checks anyway, and puts it back, and Theo watches him do that too and says nothing about that either. He does his hair, though it didn’t need it, turns to check the sweater from the side, turns back. This goes on for some time.
“Lobby, eleven-forty,” Theo says at last. “Delaney has a clipboard. Nobody has ever seen it.”

It’s ten to nine. Jack has three hours and nothing to put in them. He drags his laundry bag out from under the bed, where it has been since Sunday, and takes it down the east stairs — four, three, two, the lobby landing — and somewhere between the lobby and the basement the stairwell carries something up to him off the cinderblock.
A piano. Badly. On purpose.

s05.slug: THURSDAY · 9:00 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: From the last flight Jack hears the playing change. The length of the stairwell it has been bad on purpose — clunking, cheerful, a wrong note planted every few bars like a tell — and then, just as he reaches the bottom landing, it stops being bad. Something slow comes through the fire door instead, one phrase of it, the right hand singing and the left rolling under it, real as anything. His shoulder hits the bar. The door bangs. The phrase breaks off in the middle, and what’s left, after a decent interval, is “Heart and Soul” with one finger, at the speed of a child being made to practice.

Lena is sitting sideways on the piano bench in a gray Rosary sweatshirt with the sleeves shoved up, her boots on the seat of a folding chair and a paperback open on her knee. Her right hand is reaching back behind her to the keys, picking out the tune without looking.
“Nobody admits to playing this piano,” Jack says.
“I’m not admitting,” she says. “I’m doing laundry.”
He holds up the bag. “So am I.”

At nine on a Thursday night the basement is theirs. Eight washers, three of them working. Six dryers along the far wall, one of them going, a pair of red socks coming round in its window. Priya’s laminated sign by the door with the hours on it and CLEAN THE LINT TRAP in capitals. The vending machines humming. The upright against the cinderblock, with its dead F. On the washer beside the bench, the Community Coffee mug, clean.

Lena hooks the folding chair with her boot heel and shoves it across the concrete at him without looking up. He loads the nearest working washer — jeans, the Mooney hoodie, a week of everything he owns in gray — feeds it quarters, and sits.

body.text: “She gave me the peace too,” Lena says. “She didn’t have to.”
body.else: “She gave you the peace,” Lena says.

body: “She texted me at two.” Jack watches the washer fill. “She’s praying for me.”
Lena wets a finger and turns a page. “Course she is.”

body.text: And then, still on the page: “Does your mama know?” “Not yet.”

body: “Julian’s playing Bastille till eleven,” she says. “He’s picking me up at twenty to twelve. Laney’s forcing the whole floor.”
“I’ve been forced.”
Bastille is Thursdays. It’s Thursday. She’s down here.
Over the vending machines there’s a clock in a wire cage, and from now on Jack knows where it is without having to look.

The paperback is Laney’s *New Moon*: TEAM JACOB across the cover in silver Sharpie, Post-its sprouting off the top edge in three colors. Lena is on page four hundred. “Laney says I can’t come tonight unless I’ve read it,” she says. “I’m reading it out of spite.”
“How’s the spite holding up?”
“I got through Leviticus faster,” she says. “Leviticus had more plot.”

s06.slug: THURSDAY · 9:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: She holds the book up at him, cover out, TEAM JACOB, like a crucifix at a vampire, and waits for the sneer.
He doesn’t have one. “I’ve read it.”
“You have not.”
“All four.”

Out loud, he tells her. To Gina, the summer before senior year, on the porch steps on Glenwood Avenue — a chapter a night, and then three — because that was the summer after Danny went in, and Gina wasn’t sleeping, and it was the only thing she’d let anybody read to her. Not Ma’s *Guideposts*. Not him doing Chesterton. Bella Swan and the boy with the Volvo, under the porch light, with the moths. They were halfway through the third one when the fourth came out, and Ma drove them to a strip-mall bookstore in Boardman for the midnight release, Gina in pajama pants among two hundred girls in pajama pants, and he had to read her the first chapter in the parking lot under a light pole because she wouldn’t wait for home. Some nights she fell asleep against the porch post before the end of a chapter, and he kept reading anyway, quieter, to the end of it, because you don’t stop in the middle. One night his father came out on the porch with a Stroh’s for the vampire baseball game in the thunderstorm, listened to two pages of it, said, “That’s not how you turn a double play,” and went back inside, and Gina laughed so hard she got the hiccups, and it was the first time she’d laughed since January.
Lena knows where Danny is. She closes the book on her finger and looks at him. “And?”
“She was furious at the ending. Seven hundred pages and they all stand around in a field and *talk*. She threw it at the porch light.”
“Did you do the voices?”
“I did not do the voices.”
“You did Edward.”
“I did a little Edward.”
“Which one did you like best?”

“*Eclipse*.” He doesn’t have to think about it. “There’s a night in a tent on a mountain in a snowstorm, and she’s freezing, and the werewolf has to get in the sleeping bag and keep her alive, and the vampire has to sit in the corner of the tent and *take* it. All night. Being polite.”
Lena stares at him. “That’s the most Catholic thing you have ever said to me.”
“Gina made me read that chapter twice.”
She laughs at him, and goes on smiling after the laugh is done, with her finger still in the book. “Does she sleep now?”
“Mostly. She’s fifteen. She sleeps through first period.”
Lena and Gina are Facebook friends; Lena signs her wall posts to Gina like letters. So the next question is a serious one, and she asks it seriously. “Is she Team Edward?”
“She’s Team *Edward*. She says Jacob is literally a dog.”
“He *is* literally a dog.” Lena uncaps a pink highlighter and goes looking for the page.

s07.slug: THURSDAY · 9:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: By twenty-five to ten his washer has gone to rinse and Lena has turned round on the bench to face him with both boots planted on the concrete, and they are doing it properly. There’s no Margot down here, no marker, no Kevin with a stopwatch on his BlackBerry — two people and a dryer, and no one keeping count but them. The book is bristling. Pink, Lena explains, unprompted, is Laney for *swoon*; yellow is Laney for *problematic*, a word Laney got from Margot and now uses about everything, including the Pi Lam bylaws; green is Lena, objecting.
Jack opens with the obvious. “The prose —”

“Don’t. I know.” She holds up a hand. “The prose is a sin against the Ursulines. I’ve confessed reading it. Twice. Father Osei gave me a decade for the adverbs.” She lowers the hand. “That isn’t my argument.”

“Here’s what nobody at this school wants to hear,” she says. “It’s the only book in the world where the *boy* says no, Costigan. A hundred-year-old boy who won’t so much as kiss her properly in case it kills her, and who wants to marry her first. And millions of fourteen-year-old girls read that and decided the boy who won’t is hotter than the boy who will. A Mormon mother of three in Arizona did more for chastity in four books than a thousand youth ministers with purity rings and a PowerPoint.” She shuts the book and holds it against her chest like a missal. “Our Lady of Prompt Succor couldn’t have done better with a pamphlet.”
It’s a good argument. It’s a better argument than the one he brought down the stairs, which was that the books are bad.

“Fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, Youngstown.” Lena doesn’t blink. “Edward’s just *literal* about it.” She opens the book again. “And you’d be amazed how many boys light the match.”

response: “Everybody’s chaste at a hundred,” Jack says.
Lena laughs, peels a pink Post-it off the top of the book, and sticks it to his knee. “That’s for cheap,” she says. “I don’t score cheap.”
“You laughed.”
“I laugh at Doug Pruitt. I don’t give Doug Pruitt *points*.”

response: “The boy says no,” Jack says. “Fine. I’ll give you that. It’s rarer than vampires.”
“Thank you.” And then, because she can’t help it: “At Marisol it’s rarer than *Catholics*.”
“Catholics who mean it.”
“Don’t push your luck, Youngstown. You were doing so well.”

response: “Chastity isn’t a no,” Jack says. “Aquinas files it under temperance. It’s a yes — to the right thing, at the right time, for the right reason. Edward isn’t temperate. He’s scared.”
“Aquinas,” Lena says, “never met a boy with a Volvo.”
“Aquinas never met a *car*.”
“That’s my point. He’d have given it an entire question. *Whether the Volvo is an occasion of sin.* Objection one.”

s07a.slug: THURSDAY · 9:48 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: “Is he back yet?” Jack says. “Page four hundred. He’s got to be back.”
“Don’t you *dare*. I’m reading it in order, like a Christian.”

Across the room the washer bangs into its spin and hums against the cinderblock. Lena flips back most of the way and turns it around to show him: four pages in a row with nothing on them but a month. OCTOBER. NOVEMBER. DECEMBER. JANUARY.

“*New Moon*, though,” she says. “He leaves her. For her own good. He doesn’t ask her — he decides what’s good for her, and he goes, and she sits in a chair for four months.” She taps the empty pages, one, two, three, four. “That’s the worst thing a man can do to a woman, Jack. Decide for her and call it love.” She isn’t finished. “And everybody lets him. His family packs up the house and goes, because Edward’s decided, and not one of those vampires — and some of them have had *centuries* to think about it — says, *Has anybody asked Bella?*” She peels a green Post-it off the cover and sticks it, hard, on JANUARY.
She turns the book back around and finds her place.

choices.text: “Sometimes you stay away because you know what you’d do if you didn’t.”
response: “Sometimes you stay away,” Jack says, “because you know what you’d do if you didn’t.”
Lena looks at him over the top of the book. It goes on past the place where she would usually have an answer ready. Then she turns a page she hasn’t read.
“Then you tell her so,” she says. “You don’t run off and sulk on another continent.”

response: “He should have asked her,” Jack says.
Lena is still for a moment, with the book open on her knee and her thumb on the page.
“Yes,” she says.
She says nothing else. She reads on.

response: “Then a werewolf fixes her up a motorcycle,” Jack says. “Seems like it worked out.”
“Do *not* say that in front of Laney.” Lena points the highlighter at him. “She’ll put you on a T-shirt. In glitter. She has the iron-on letters, Jack, I’ve *seen* them.”

s07b.slug: THURSDAY · 10:02 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: By two minutes past ten they’ve run out of Post-its to point with. Somebody on an upper floor flushes, and the water goes down through the wall behind the dryers like a heckler leaving early.
“At the Rosary,” Lena says, “half the junior class read these under the desks in Religion. Sister Agnes confiscated eleven copies and read every one of them. For safety.”
“Sister Agnes was Team Edward.”
“Sister Agnes was Team *Charlie*. She liked a man with a mustache who minded his own business.”
“So that’s why they read it,” Jack says. “For the waiting.”
“No.”
When she makes her last move she isn’t looking at him. She’s watching her dryer, the red socks coming round in the window and dropping and coming round.

“It isn’t about waiting at all,” she says. “Not really. Not the ring, not the rules. Every girl reading it wants one thing. To be the one somebody can’t stay away from — so much that a hundred years of good manners go out the window the day she walks into biology.”

choices.text: “Then it’s a prayer with a vampire in it.”
response: “Then it’s a prayer,” Jack says. “With a vampire in it.”
Lena turns from the dryer and nods at him slowly, like it’s a better answer than she had ready. “Okay,” she says. “Okay. I’ll take that.”

choices.text: “Then he’s the villain of the book. He stayed away.”
response: “Then he’s the villain of the book,” Jack says. “He stayed away.”

“Oh, he’s a *terrible* boyfriend,” Lena says, still watching the socks. “I never said he wasn’t. That’s why they love him. They’re not stupid, Jack. They just want somebody to stay away from them that *hard*.”

choices.text: “Laney’s going to be very upset you left Jacob out of it.”
response: “Laney’s going to be very upset you left Jacob out of it,” Jack says. “He never stays away. He’s right *there*. With his shirt off.”
Lena opens her mouth, and shuts it, and swings round on the bench and points at him with the highlighter, grinning. “You just *forfeited*.”

s08.slug: THURSDAY · 10:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: At half past ten her dryer buzzes — the Delgado dryers don’t finish so much as complain — and stops. She folds on top of the washer: a black-and-gold Saints T-shirt washed soft as a dishrag, the oatmeal cardigan — she holds it up to the light, frowns at the hole in one elbow, and folds it anyway. The towels she leaves in a warm heap for later. “Mémère irons dish towels,” she says, smoothing the Saints shirt flat on the washer lid. “And pillowcases. And one Easter, Daddy’s twenty-dollar bills, so they’d be nice for the collection.” Jack watches her hands on the shirt, and then makes himself look at the vending machines.
Then she sits down at the upright, the right way round this time, facing it, and picks out a phrase with one finger. Slow, wrong, the top line of something that wants two hands and is getting one.
“This is the vampire song,” she says. “According to Laney. Laney also thinks the Pope can veto movies, so.” She plays the phrase again, worse. “Did you see what she put Theo in?”
“Jacob, under cashmere. For deniability. He showed me.” Jack leans on the washer. “It’s a lot of deniability.”
“Laney says if he takes the sweater off in the theater she’ll know the movie *worked*.”

choices.text: “Play it right. Once.”
response: “Play it right,” Jack says. “Once.”
She looks at him over her shoulder, and he waits for the joke, and it doesn’t come. She turns back to the keys and puts both hands on them.

choices.text: “Play it like Edward would. Brooding. In a Volvo.”
response: “Play it like Edward would,” Jack says. “Brooding. In a Volvo.”

She gives him three bars of Edward — shoulders up around her ears, chin down, glowering at the keys like they’ve insulted her family — and laughs at herself, and stops laughing, and starts again from the top.

choices.text: Fold her towels. Say nothing.
response: He takes the second towel off the pile and folds it. He folds it wrong — in half, in half again, Glenwood Avenue style — and she gets up, takes it out of his hands, refolds it in thirds and sets it on the stack.
Then she sits back down at the upright. He hasn’t said a word.

s08a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:36 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: It’s “Clair de lune.” Jack knows it the way everybody knows it — movies, commercials, the radio in a dentist’s office — and he has never heard it in a room.

First she sits a moment with her hands in her lap, the way Rosie sits before she says grace, as though she’s waiting on permission from somebody. Then she plays it slower than the radio does. Her right hand carries the tune and her left goes down under it and comes back up, and her shoulders come down from around her ears, and the bench creaks when she leans into the place where it opens out. She watches the keys, and then her eyes are on nothing in the room. And every few bars the tune walks onto the dead F and there’s nothing — a felt hammer on a string that won’t answer, a hole the size of one note — and she doesn’t stop for it or reach around it. She leaves the hole. The music goes on on both sides of it, and Jack hears the missing note anyway, because everything around it is so sure the note belongs there. Then it comes round again.
Near the end the compressor in the Coke machine kicks on and hums under her, and she plays over it.
Jack doesn’t move. If he moves she might remember he’s there.
When it’s done she keeps her hands on the keys until the last chord has gone out of the strings. Then she puts them in her lap.
Jack lifts his hands to clap.
“Don’t you dare,” she says.
He puts them down. “That,” he says, “was not badly.”
“No.”
“The Rosary-girl thing. Three in the morning, playing it wrong so nobody suspects.”
“That’s what I tell people.” She flexes her fingers, one hand and then the other. “If you play well, people ask you to play.”

body.text: “You asked.” “I asked.”
“You asked. More or less.” “I asked.”
“You didn’t even ask.” “I didn’t.”

body: “The last time I played it right in front of anybody,” she says, “was in November. Four years ago.”
She doesn’t say where. He doesn’t ask.

body: Her hand goes up to the medal at her collar, rests there, and comes back down to the keys. She plays the first two bars again, quietly, as far as the dead F, and stops there.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 11:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: They talk until the caged clock says a quarter past eleven: the nun at the Rosary who hit the music stand with a ruler and never the child; Laney’s Post-it key, written out on an index card and folded into Laney’s wallet behind her fake ID; whether the Delgado dryers are possessed or only Protestant; whether Our Lady of Prompt Succor has ever been asked to do anything about the Browns, and whether she’d even consider it. His laundry tumbles. Hers sits folded on the washer with the book on top.
Then she shows him the dead F. She scoots down to make room, and he sits beside her on a bench built for one and a half, shoulder to shoulder, his knee against the side of the keyboard.
“That one.” She presses it. The key goes down, the hammer goes, and nothing happens. “Dead since before Priya. Every piano’s got one note that won’t. That’s this one’s.”

Jack considers the dead F. He cracks his knuckles. He shakes out his wrists for Carnegie Hall, lifts his right hand high over the keyboard, holds it there with his eyes shut — and brings one finger down on the dead F, tenderly, and holds it, swaying a little, while it makes no sound at all.

Lena goes. She laughs so hard she has to grab his arm to keep from sliding off the end of the bench, and she’s still hanging on to it, gasping, when she says, “Again,” and he does it again, softer — the sad part — with a little vibrato on nothing.

She wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand. Then she reaches across to show him how it’s really done, the dead F with some wrist in it, and his finger is still on the key, and hers comes down on top of it. The same key. The same octave. She doesn’t take it away, and for the length of a breath he can feel her pulse in the side of her finger, or his own.
He wants her. On a bench this size it isn’t complicated.

choices.text: Slide your hand down an octave. Play her the bass half of “Heart and Soul.”
response: He slides his hand out from under hers and down to the bottom of the keyboard and starts the bass half of “Heart and Soul,” the four chords every kid learns first.

Lena takes the top without being asked. They play it badly together, on purpose, louder every time round, until the vending machine rattles — and she ends it, because of course she does, on the dead F.

choices.text: Don’t move your hand when hers finds the same key.
choices.key: On the piano bench, when Lena’s hand found the same key, you didn’t move yours.
response: Jack doesn’t move his hand.

choices.text: “This was a good night.”
response: “This was a good night,” Jack says.
Lena looks down at their two hands on the one key. Then she takes hers back into her lap.
“It was,” she says. And then, because she’s Lena: “Don’t you tell Laney I played.”

s09j.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: At twenty to twelve the door at the top of the stairs opens and Julian Park-Ellis is standing in it: a cardigan that was somebody’s father’s, car keys in one hand, the guitar case with the BART sticker in the other, straight from Bastille. He doesn’t come down.
“Lena? We’ll miss the vampires.” He finds Jack and nods to him, friendly, meaning it. “You coming? There’s room in the car.”
“I’m going with the floor,” Jack says.
“Sure. See you there.”

Lena gets up. She stacks the folded laundry in her basket, sets Laney’s book on top with its Post-its fluttering, and hooks the Community Coffee mug on one finger. At the bottom step she turns round. “Go on up, Youngstown,” she says. “Laney’s taking attendance.” She goes up the stairs with the basket on her hip, and at the top Julian takes the basket from her, and the lobby comes down the stairwell at them — somebody up there is already shrieking about capes — and the last thing Jack hears is Julian asking if she finished the book, and Lena saying she’s reading it out of spite, and Julian laughing like he’s glad to know it.

body.text: Jack is still on the bench. The fallboard is down over the keys, where she put it.
body.else: Jack is still on the bench. The keys are open, all eighty-eight of them, one of them dead.

body: His dryer has stopped. Hers, when he gets up and puts his hand on the drum, is empty and still warm.

s09r.slug: THURSDAY · 11:22 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: Neither of them plays the key. Her fingers lie along the back of his, on ivory that wouldn’t make a sound if they did. The clock in its cage gets to twenty past and keeps going. He can smell the dryer sheets on her sleeve. He wants to turn his hand over under hers and hold it, and he doesn’t, and he doesn’t take it away either.

Lena breathes in once, slowly. Then she reaches across him with her other hand and draws the fallboard down over the keys — slowly, slowly enough that both their hands are under the edge of it, and then they aren’t — and it comes to rest on the keys with a soft wooden knock.
She leaves her hand on the lid.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 12:01 AM · THE RIALTO, MISSION STREET
body: At a minute past midnight the biggest of the four houses the Rialto got cut into in 1987 — the one that kept the old proscenium — is full to the back wall and sounds like a pep rally. The line was around the block at a quarter to twelve: capes, mostly, and Team shirts, a girl who had come as Bella’s red truck in a painted refrigerator box on shoulder straps, and a boy with glitter all over his face who told anyone who looked at him that it was for accuracy.

Laney has run the floor through all of it like a pageant director with a show to bring in on time. Head count in the lobby at eleven-forty; head count in the Odyssey; head count on the sidewalk under the marquee, where NEW MOON 12:01 · SOLD OUT is spelled in the old black letters with one of the O’s borrowed from a 6; tickets dealt out of her clutch one at a time. Jack never sees the clipboard. He sees what it does. Theo, Jacob under cashmere. Margot, in black, who informed the Odyssey on the way over that she was here to observe a fertility rite. Doug, who has never seen a Twilight anything and said *dude* at the line the way other people say *amen*. Kevin, who drove — “I’m the designated adult,” he told the girl at the ticket window, who hadn’t asked. And Jack.

Margot, taking her seat with her notebook on her knee, surveys the house — three hundred girls and the boys who drove them — and delivers her findings to nobody in particular. “Every culture has one. A ritual in which the young are told that wanting is dangerous, and then sold a poster of it.”

body.text: Kevin takes the seat beside Jack without a word.

body: In the lobby Julian had found them — the cardigan, his car keys, Lena beside him — and Laney had said, sweet as a hostess at a garden party, “Lovely set list, Julian. *Very* well organized.” Julian thanked her, because he’s Julian. Jack had seen her earlier at the concession stand, standing very close to Julian’s elbow while he paid for Lena’s Junior Mints. There is a sheet of notebook paper folded in her clutch now, sticking up out of the clasp.
She slides into the seat beside Jack and settles the clutch in her lap. “Now that you’re back on the *market*, sugar —”
“No.”
In the row ahead, a little to the left, are Lena and Julian.
On Laney’s far side Theo says, not quite under his breath, “Edward, with a capo.”
Kevin leans forward to find him down the row. “Respectfully. Leave it alone.”

choices.text: Say nothing.
response: Jack watches the curtain. Theo glances over at him and takes the silence for permission, and then is quiet anyway, because the lights go down and the trailers start, and somebody three rows back shushes the entire theater on principle.

choices.text: “He’s Jacob, if anything. He’s *warm*.”
response: “He’s Jacob, if anything,” Jack says. “He’s *warm*.”
Laney laughs — one bark — and is furious about it, and sits up straight to check the back of Lena’s head, which hasn’t turned. Theo looks at Jack with something close to love. The lights go down.

choices.text: “Theo.”
response: “Theo,” Jack says. Just that.
Theo shuts up for exactly one trailer. Down the row Kevin settles back in his seat with his arms folded, and the lights go the rest of the way down.

s10a.slug: FRIDAY · 12:40 AM · THE RIALTO, MISSION STREET
body: Edward leaves in the first act, in the woods, in the rain, and the Rialto takes it personally. A girl somewhere in the middle says *no* like she means it. Then the picture goes quiet, and there is Bella in a chair at her bedroom window, and the camera goes slowly around and around her while the months go by outside the glass, each one with its name on the screen. OCTOBER. NOVEMBER. The trees go bare. The glass goes white. She doesn’t get up.
Somewhere around December, in the row ahead, Lena puts her head on Julian’s shoulder.

It looks like a good shoulder for it. She’s still there through the snow; he can see the top of her head against the cardigan, and the light off the screen moving in her hair. Jack watches the screen. He watches it very carefully, the girl in the chair, for the rest of the winter.

Laney grips Jack’s forearm through the motorcycle sequence and will deny it afterward. When Jacob takes his shirt off to wipe the blood off Bella’s forehead the theater screams like the roof is coming in, and Margot, in the dark, writes something down. Later the wolves come out of the trees, and Lena sneezes once, into Julian’s cardigan, and four seats down Doug says *bless you* at a normal speaking volume.
At twenty past two the lights come up on a lobby full of capes going home, everybody blinking. Somebody’s fangs are on the carpet by the popcorn machine.

body.text: By the poster for *2012*, Julian has his keys out and Lena’s coat over his arm, and he stops beside Jack on his way to find her. “I put the second chorus back,” he says. “Tonight.”
“How’d it go?”
“Long,” Julian says, and smiles, and goes.

body: Kevin jingles the Odyssey’s keys at him from the door. “There’s room, Jack. Doug folds.”
“I’m going to walk.”

Kevin looks at him for a second and doesn’t argue. So Jack walks home down Mission Street at half past two in the morning, three miles, with his hands in the Carhartt — past Bastille with its chairs up on the tables and the chalkboard turned to the wall, past the Walgreens, still lit — and every block or so a vampire is unlocking a Civic.

body: He’s on four hours of sleep and the Rialto’s popcorn. At the first light on Mission he texts Gina back, one key at a time: *agreed. dog.*

It’s three miles to the wharf on La Flaca with the wind in his face. Rudy lifts a spatula at him from the flat-top. Gloria fills a quart of the chicken and rice before he’s finished asking, snaps the lid on, and drops it in a paper sack with a sleeve of saltines. “For the pecan,” she says. “Tell her it’s from me.” He rides it back up Mission Street in the basket with one hand on the sack at every light.
217’s door is open. There’s a campus-clinic flyer about H1N1 taped to it at Laney’s eye level, with *FEVER = GO HOME* circled twice in pink.

Lena is in bed under the quilt in a Mardi Gras sweatshirt — purple, green and gold, the fleur-de-lis cracked from the wash — with a box of Kleenex at her hip and her laptop on her knees, and her nose is red, and she is saying, “It’s a *cold*, Laney, I took my temperature, it’s ninety-nine-point-*nothing*,” to Laney, who is lying on her own bed with a nail file and a folded sheet of lined paper, a list of song titles in somebody’s neat capitals; she keeps turning it over and smoothing it on her stomach. Margot is in the desk chair in black, with a printout stapled at the corner and marked up in red.

And Julian is there. He’s sitting on the floor with his back against Lena’s bed and his cardigan sleeves pushed up, unscrewing a tall steel thermos with a dent in the side. Steam comes off it, rice and ginger and sesame. “My mom’s,” he’s saying. “Juk. For colds. She’d disown me if I brought you canned.”
Jack is in the doorway with the Anchor’s quart.
“*Jack* brought the *Anchor*,” Laney announces, sitting straight up on her bed, a pageant host with a surprise finalist.
Two soups.

Lena sees him and her face goes bright. “*Jack*. Is that the *Anchor*?” She holds out both hands, and he crosses and puts the sack in them. She holds the quart a moment in her lap, warm through the paper, and says “Gloria” the way other people say a saint’s name. Then she sets it on the windowsill beside the bed, carefully, label out. “For tomorrow,” she says. “I’m going to want it *tomorrow*.” And she takes the bowl Julian has poured her, and the spoon, and eats. The quart sits on the sill with the afternoon behind it, a strip of masking tape across the lid that says PECAN in Gloria’s capitals.
She’s glad Julian is there. It’s on her, plain as the cold.
Laney’s nail file stops.
Jack puts his empty hands in his pockets.

“You walked home last night,” Julian says to him, looking up from the floor. “I saw you wave off Kevin’s van. All of Mission Street, at two-thirty?” “It was a nice night.” “It was,” Julian says, and sounds like he noticed it too.
“If it’s a hundred by tonight you’re going to the clinic,” Laney tells Lena, “and I’m carrying you, and I’m wearing the mask.” “It’s not going to be a hundred.” “Then I’ll wear the mask for fun.”

On the laptop, when Lena turns it round to show him, is a long page of names, and hers is the last one on it. “The Manhattan Declaration,” she says, through the cold. “It came out this morning. Life, marriage, religious liberty — Orthodox, evangelicals, us. I signed it for the last part.” She blows her nose. “They say if the law tells them to help kill somebody, they won’t do it, and they’ll take what comes. Caesar can have everything that’s Caesar’s and not one thing that’s God’s. Dorothy Day went to jail, Jack. These men are promising to go.”

“These men,” Margot says, “are archbishops. Not one of them is going to jail. They’re going to a fundraiser.” She turns a page of the printout. “And I’d take it more seriously if it didn’t do this. The marriage section puts two men in Portland who’d like to file a joint return in the same paragraph as the unborn child, in the same tone of voice, as if they were the same kind of claim, and then it ties them in one bundle and calls the bundle *conscience* — so that anyone who disagrees with the second is persecuting you about the first. It’s coalition maintenance dressed up as moral philosophy.” She caps her red pen. “It’s very well done. That’s what bothers me.”
“It’s the same question,” Lena says. “What a body is *for*. They just answer it in one breath.”
“That’s my point.”
“Then we disagree about what a body’s for, Margot. We’ve disagreed about it since September.” Lena sniffs. “I signed it anyway.”
Julian has been listening to all of it with his arms around his knees. Now he looks up at Lena and asks her, because he really wants to know, “What would you go to jail for?”

Lena puts the spoon down. She thinks about it — actually thinks — and then she tells him, and it takes the rest of the bowl. If they made it a crime to feed people under the Claiborne overpass, she’d go. If a girl wanted to keep her baby and everybody with a clipboard was telling her she couldn’t afford to, Lena would go with her, wherever that was. If they ever made a nurse hand somebody the pill or the needle, she’d go with the nurse. “Not for a bishop’s feelings,” she says. “I wouldn’t go to jail for a bishop’s feelings.”
Julian listens to every word. When she’s done he doesn’t argue with any of it. He says, “Okay,” like it’s something about her he means to keep, and fills her bowl again from the thermos.
It’s a good question. Jack wishes he’d been the one to ask it.
Then Lena tips the laptop toward the doorway. “Costigan?”

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog.

choices.text: “Give me the laptop.”
choices.key: Friday Lena signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed with a cold. You signed it too.
response: “Give me the laptop,” Jack says.
Lena passes it to him over Julian’s head, and Jack types his name standing up, hunting for the letters, and hands it back.
“Welcome to the resistance, Costigan,” Lena says. “Bring a toothbrush.”
From the desk chair, Margot: “Two useful idiots. One laptop.”

choices.text: “I’ll sign the part about the baby. I won’t promise a website I’ll break the law.”
choices.key: Friday you told Lena you’d sign the part about the baby — but you won’t promise a website you’ll break the law.
response: “I’ll sign the part about the baby,” Jack says. “I won’t promise a website I’ll break the law.”
Lena stares at him over the Kleenex. “*Youngstown*. You’d go to jail for *nothing*?”
“I’d go to jail for something. I just won’t promise it in advance. To a website.”
“Somebody note the date,” Margot says. “He’s being reasonable. It’s terrifying.”

choices.text: To Margot: “You’re right that it isn’t the same kind of claim.” Then sign.
choices.key: Friday you told Margot she was right about the marriage section — and signed the Declaration anyway.
response: “You’re right,” Jack tells Margot. “It isn’t the same kind of claim.”
Then he takes the laptop off Lena’s knees and signs it.
Margot, who is not often thrown, is thrown. “Then why *sign*?”
“Because the rest of it’s right.”
Lena blows her nose at both of them.

s12.slug: FRIDAY · 5:50 PM · THE 2ND-FLOOR HALL → THE EAST STAIRS
body: Julian goes first, at a quarter to six, with the empty thermos under his arm; he has a rehearsal, he says, and he’ll come back at nine with tea. On his way past the bed he touches Lena’s hair.
Five minutes later Jack and Margot go too. Margot pulls 217’s door to behind them and it doesn’t catch — the latch has never quite met the plate — and it drifts back open a hand’s width on the hall.
Inside, Laney is talking, low and fast, too low to make out. It has the shape of something she’s been saving all afternoon.
Then Lena, stuffed up and patient and perfectly clear: “—Laney, he *ended* it. People are sad when they end things. Even when they’re the one who does it.”
Jack is still standing there with his hand half out for the knob when somebody inside pushes the door shut.
Margot is already at the east stairs. Jack follows her down. A flight below, without turning round, she says it.
“He brought her his mother’s porridge, and he asked her what she’d go to jail for, and then he listened.” Another step. “He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.”
“I’ve done a great deal of fieldwork on couples,” she says, “most of it at my parents’ kitchen table. That one doesn’t need a footnote.”
She isn’t being clever. She means it.
“I know,” Jack says. He does know. He watched the man fill her bowl.
Margot nods, once, as though he’s confirmed a source.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it.

body: Laney is lying across Theo’s bed with her shoes kicked off on the rug and her ankles crossed on his pillow, and Theo is at the window with his iPhone to his ear, using his telephone manners.
“Harbor Inn? Vance. Cancel the Costigan. Saturday, eight. — No. Nothing’s wrong with the piano. The piano is beyond reproach.” He listens. “You’re very kind. I’m sure she will.”
Laney addresses the ceiling. “We are being *punished*.”
Jack is in the doorway with his towel over his shoulder and his shower caddy in his hand, back from the end of the hall. “Punished for what?”
“*New Moon*, fireman,” Laney says, without looking. “Two hours of a girl in a chair.”
Theo hangs up. “My mother can’t come up.” He sets the phone face down on the desk with the air of a man retiring a story with honors.
Then Theo looks at Laney, and Laney turns her head on the pillow and looks back at Theo, and something gets decided in the space over the rug that Jack isn’t part of. Theo opens his closet.

“Pruitt is raiding,” he announces, going through hangers. “Tran is studying. Lindqvist is reading something in German to spite us. Delaney has a prior engagement with a box of Kleenex. Which leaves you, and me, and my car. Get dressed.”
He holds out a shirt on a hanger: charcoal, soft as a dish towel, with some Japanese label stitched inside the collar. “It’s mine. By the end of the night it’ll be yours. They always are.”
“Theo, I’m not —”
“You’ve been sad about Becca for two days,” Theo says, with a straight face, “and very convincing. I’d like a night off from it.”
“Where are we going?”

“A party. In Montecito. Somebody’s parents’ house, and the somebody’s parents are in London. A pool nobody swims in, a view of the entire Channel, and a kitchen the size of the Fishbowl.” Theo hangs the shirt on Jack’s closet door himself and steps back from it. “And let me be very clear, because I know how your mind works. This is not a setup. I am not setting you up. I’m *forbidding* it. Tonight you stand in a kitchen and let rich people bore you, and you remember you’re nineteen.”
“Eighteen.”
“Details.” Theo looks over at Jack’s boots by the bed. “Those can come. Those have character. Nothing else you own is invited.”

Laney swings her feet down and starts working them back into her flats. “And if you so much as learn a girl’s name tonight,” she says, “I will have you killed. I’ve thought about the method. It’s very clean.”
“Why?”
Theo answers for her, getting his camel coat off its hanger. “She feels you’re fragile.”
Jack looks from one of them to the other. Theo is buttoning the coat. Laney is studying a thumbnail.

Laney stands up and smooths her skirt and gives Jack the full pageant smile. It ought to worry him. On her way out she takes the box of Kleenex off Theo’s desk — the good kind, with the lotion — and tucks it under her arm for the sick girl downstairs.

choices.text: “Does the shirt come with a personality?”
response: “Does the shirt come with a personality?”
“It comes with *mine*,” Theo says. “Return both by Monday.” He tosses Jack a stick of his deodorant, unrequested, and checks his own hair in the mirror one last time.

choices.text: “I’m bad company tonight, Theo.”
response: “I’m bad company tonight, Theo.”
Theo doesn’t make a joke out of it. He takes the shirt off the closet door and puts the hanger in Jack’s hand. “I know,” he says. “That’s why I’m bringing you to people who won’t notice.”

choices.text: “Give me the shirt.”
response: “Give me the shirt.”
Laney, in the doorway with the Kleenex, gives him one slow clap, like the back row at a pageant. Theo hands it over with a small bow.

body: Theo takes the 101 south with the top down in November, the heater roaring at their shins and the cold going straight down the back of Jack’s borrowed collar. A cassette adapter runs from the old Becker deck to the iPhone in the cupholder, and Randy Newman is telling Los Angeles he loves it, and Theo is telling it with him — every word, the shouted parts too — with no irony at all. It’s the face he keeps for the last ten minutes of *Point Break*.

For forty minutes the ocean is on their right, black all the way out, with the train tracks running between. Santa Barbara comes up in a long low scatter of lights along the water and goes by, and a mile past it Theo takes an exit Jack didn’t see coming and starts to climb. Montecito turns out to be hedges: twelve feet of them, dark on both sides of a lane with no sidewalk and no streetlights, broken every so often by a gate and a call box and a number cut in stone. There’s no moon. Below them Jack can tell where the sea is only by where the lights stop.

“Wyatt Halloran,” Theo says, turning the music down for the pitch. “Junior. Two years ahead of me at Harvard-Westlake, where he was voted Most Likely to Own a Boat, and does. His father has produced three of the worst films of the decade for my father’s people. This is the house the second one built. They use it six weekends a year. Tonight Wyatt has invited everyone he’s ever met between here and Malibu.”
My father’s people is Meridian. Jack has been on two expeditions on its letterhead.
“What was the second one?”
“A golden retriever gets elected to the Senate. I’ve seen it four times.” Theo downshifts for a hairpin between two walls of hedge. “Think of it as penance, Father Jack. I do.”

At the top the lane gives out into a gravel turnaround and a house made mostly of light: glass walls lit gold from inside, a flat slab of roof, the front of it pushed out over a canyon on nothing Jack can see. Two black cars with Los Angeles dealer frames sit in the turnaround with their drivers in them and the engines off. Theo parks the SL beside them, nose out, and kills the ignition, and Randy Newman stops in the middle of a word.

On the front step Theo’s face changes. It goes smooth and pleasant and about ten years older — a face for valets, and for the people who tip them. Then the door opens on noise and warm air, and Theo puts a hand between Jack’s shoulder blades and walks him in.

s15.slug: FRIDAY · 10:55 PM · THE HALLORAN HOUSE, MONTECITO, THE POOL DECK
body: The house is one idea, executed in money: glass and board-formed concrete cantilevered out over the canyon, and at the end of the deck a pool lit so blue Jack could read by it, and past the pool the hill falls away through the oaks to the whole Santa Barbara Channel — the city strung along the water to the west, and then nothing, the dark where the ocean is, all the way out to where the islands must be. Passion Pit is coming out of speakers hidden in the planters, a falsetto riding a drum machine, and around the pool stand forty people who all seem to have gone to the same four schools. They hold their drinks low and loose, like something they’re walking for somebody else.
A girl at the sliding door puts an empty red cup in Jack’s hand by way of a wristband, and Theo loses him in three minutes, by being Theo.

First a girl in a sequined top finds him by the outdoor kitchen — “Theo, thank God, Jordan’s in the powder room, it’s the callback, they went with the *other* girl” — and Theo produces a cocktail napkin from his coat pocket, monogrammed, and says something low that stops her chin shaking. Then a tall boy in a backwards Dodgers cap comes through the crowd with a cordless phone pressed to his chest. “Vance. The neighbor again. Noise. She wants an adult.” “Wyatt, I’m nineteen.” “You’re the closest thing.” Then a producer’s son in a fedora has an idea about a vampire who works in finance, and Theo is being steered toward the far end of the deck with a hand on each elbow.
He calls back over his shoulder. “Stay here. Don’t move. Don’t talk to anybody with a headshot.”

Jack stays. He stands by the outdoor kitchen, which is the size of the Fishbowl, as advertised, with two ovens in it nobody has ever turned on, and listens to Los Angeles talk. A boy’s manager says pilot season is going to be a bloodbath. A girl has booked a cell-phone commercial and is being congratulated in a tone usually kept for funerals. Somebody’s father is on a board; somebody else’s father is on a boat. A girl with a clipboard under her arm, who may or may not work here, looks at the empty cup and then at him.
“Who are you with?”
“Theo Vance.”
She nods, as though that accounts for the shirt. “And who reps you?”
“The Diocese of Youngstown.”
She laughs, politely, and seems to decide he’s somebody’s cousin, and goes.

When Jack looks again Theo is a camel coat at the far end of the pool with his LA face on, laughing at something the fedora said, holding the same glass of bourbon somebody handed him at the door. It’s still full. He’s driving.
Jack stands at the rail with his empty cup, over a canyon full of dark, in a house where nobody knows his name. It’s less restful than Lena made it sound.

choices.text: Wyatt’s tequila, because it’s handed to you.
response: Wyatt comes back past the pool with the cordless phone under one arm and a bottle of Patrón in the other hand, pouring for anybody holding still, and Jack is holding still. Wyatt fills the bottom of the red cup without asking his name — “Welcome, man” — and goes off after Theo.

Jack drinks it because it’s there. It goes down hot and finds a place behind his breastbone to sit, and for a minute the deck is easier to stand on. Then the minute is over, and the falsetto is still going, and the clipboard girl has written him off as a cousin, and he wants a room with a door in it. Inside, a staircase goes down into the house — slabs of pale oak floating off the wall with nothing under them — and Jack takes it, looking for quiet.

choices.text: One beer. Make it last an hour.
response: There’s a galvanized tub of Pacifico on ice by the outdoor kitchen. Jack takes one, pours it into the red cup so nobody can count his bottles, and gives it an hour. He stands at the rail and sips and watches the far end of the deck, where Theo is being pitched at with both hands, and the hour doesn’t get any shorter.

Ten minutes of it is enough. He wants a room with a door in it. Inside, a staircase goes down into the house — slabs of pale oak floating off the wall with nothing under them — and Jack takes it, looking for quiet.

choices.text: A Coke from the bar fridge.
response: The bar fridge under the outdoor counter is full of bottles with labels in French. Jack asks the girl standing next to it whether there’s any pop.

She turns and looks at him with real interest. She has a nose ring and a cardigan that cost more than his bus ticket home. “You’re very *Midwestern*,” she says, not unkindly, and digs him out a Coke from behind the Perrier.

He pours it into the red cup so it looks like something. It fools no one, and the girl has already gone back to her friends. Ten minutes at the rail is enough; he wants a room with a door in it. Inside, a staircase goes down into the house — slabs of pale oak floating off the wall with nothing under them — and Jack takes it, looking for quiet.

s16.slug: FRIDAY · 11:50 PM · THE HALLORAN HOUSE, THE DEN
body: The house goes down the hill in levels, and it takes Jack most of an hour to find the bottom of it: a hall of framed movie posters for movies he has never heard of, three of them for the same movie in three languages; a gym with a rowing machine and nobody rowing; a bathroom with a window in the shower that looks straight down into the canyon. Above him the pool deck keeps going without him. The bass comes down through the concrete into the stair treads, felt more than heard, like weather in the next county.

Up there, three different people asked him what he does, and when he said philosophy each of them said “Oh, *fun*,” in a tone better suited to a diagnosis, and moved along to somebody who could get them something. For an hour not one person has asked him if he’s okay. He has been grateful for every minute of it, and it still adds up to an hour.

body.text: Wyatt’s tequila has settled into a low warm hum at the back of his skull, the kind that makes another flight of stairs seem like a good idea.
The beer in his hand is two-thirds gone and going warm, on schedule.
He’s on his second Coke, sweating through the can into his palm, and he can feel it in his teeth.

body: The last flight is slabs of concrete stuck into the wall with nothing under them and no rail on the open side, the stairs a man builds when he doesn’t expect anybody he loves to get old. Halfway down, two Marisol girls he half knows from the Commons are coming up, sophomores, holding their cups in front of them like they were told not to spill on anything, and the one in front is looking back down over her shoulder.
“— it’s *Cassidy*, I swear to God —”
“Don’t *look*.”
They go past him in a gust of vanilla body spray. Whoever Cassidy is, she’s their business. Jack goes on down.

The den is a long low room at the bottom of everything, carpeted the color of wet sand. A sectional the size of a fishing boat holds six people watching something with the sound off — men in suits at a desk, a score crawling along the bottom of the screen. There is a fireplace nobody has lit. The far wall is glass from the floor to the ceiling, and past it the canyon drops away into nothing at all, so the room seems to be hanging out over the dark on somebody’s word.
In the corner, where the glass meets the side wall, there’s a window seat with cushions on it, and on the window seat, alone, a girl.

She has her knees up and a paperback bent open over one of them. A man’s flannel, washed soft, the sleeves shoved past her elbows; cutoffs over black tights; bare feet, one ankle in a braided anklet. Her boots stand on the carpet by the seat, side by side, like two dogs told to stay. Her hair is long and streaked by the sun and stiff at the ends from salt water, and she’s tan in November, with freckles across her nose that she has left alone. There’s a Sharpie in her teeth, uncapped, and three highlighters in one fist, and no red cup anywhere near her. She isn’t reading the book so much as fighting it. The margins are black with her writing, and from across the room he can make out a word in capitals.

While he watches she reads a line under her breath, then reads it again a different way, then a third way with her chin up — three women trying on the same coat — and writes something beside it and underlines it hard enough to tear the page.

The room is careful about her. Six heads on the sectional, and not one of them turns toward the corner; a guy comes down for the bar fridge under the TV and goes back up without his eyes ever getting as far as the window seat. Jack reads it as anybody from Glenwood Avenue would: she wants to be left alone, and the room is doing her the courtesy.
She is the most beautiful person in the house, and she is having an argument with a book.
She takes the Sharpie out of her teeth long enough to tell nobody in particular, “God, she’s *awful*.” She writes something hard in the margin, and caps it, and uncaps it again. “She deserves it.”

The cover is turned toward him. It’s the Harvest paperback, the same edition as the Mooney castoff that rode in his back pocket all September: *A Good Man Is Hard to Find*. The word in capitals is LIAR, and it’s next to the grandmother, and it’s the third one he can see. Somebody in this house has that old woman down as a fraud from the first page to the ditch, and is defending the position in Sharpie, and is wrong.

Every room at Marisol so far, somebody else has walked him into — Theo through the door of his first party, Laney round the Lagoon by the elbow, Becca onto her team with a clipboard, Hale to a seminar table by roster. This one he crosses on his own feet: over the carpet, behind the sectional and six heads that don’t turn, into the cold that comes off the glass.

choices.text: Straight over. Sit on the far end of the window seat.
choices.key: At Wyatt Halloran’s party you crossed the room yourself.
response: He doesn’t stop at the edge of the cushions. He sits down on the far end of the window seat with his back against the glass, near enough that the paperback is within reach and far enough that it’s still a question, and the cold of the canyon comes straight through Theo’s shirt into his spine.
She doesn’t look up. She turns a page with the highlighter fist and goes on writing.

choices.text: Two waters from the bar fridge first. Hold one out.
choices.key: At Wyatt Halloran’s party you crossed the room yourself.
response: He detours to the bar fridge under the TV, where somebody’s parents keep little square bottles of Fiji in rows like a hotel, and takes two, and crosses with one held out in front of him into the space over her book.
She takes it without looking up. She turns the cap once with her thumb until she feels the seal crack, and drinks half of it, and stands the bottle on the sill against the glass.

choices.text: From the edge of the rug: “Who deserves it?”
choices.key: At Wyatt Halloran’s party you crossed the room yourself.
response: He stops at the edge of the rug, where the window seat’s territory seems to begin.
“Who deserves it?”
The Sharpie stops.

s17.slug: FRIDAY · 11:55 PM · THE HALLORAN HOUSE, THE DEN, THE WINDOW SEAT
body: She looks up.

It isn’t a long look, but it goes all the way in, and for as long as it lasts there isn’t anything else in the house: not the bass, not the men at their silent desk, not the six heads, not the charcoal shirt he’s wearing that isn’t his. He has been looked at a good deal this week. Theo has looked at him, and Laney has, and Gloria. They were all looking at what happened to him. She’s looking at him — here, on a Friday, at five to twelve, with nothing behind it — like he’s the news. For a second he forgets what he was going to say next.

“Shh,” she says. For a second she’s a librarian, sixty, with a pencil through her bun and a card catalog at her back; he can see all of it, and she hasn’t moved anything but her mouth. Then the librarian is gone and it’s a girl in a window seat with a Sharpie.

body.text: “You’re on my window seat.” “It’s a big window seat.” “It’s a big book,” she says, and seems to think that settles it in her favor.
She tips the bottle at him. “Thank you for the water. Brave choice. Everybody else down here brings tequila.”
“The grandmother,” she says. “Obviously. Sit down, you’re making the window nervous.” He sits, on the far end of the seat, with the glass cold at his back.

body: She holds the book up so he can see the damage. “I’m reading for a part. A preacher’s daughter, in a movie that’s ‘very O’Connor,’ the director says. Directors say that when they read one story in college. So I’m reading O’Connor.” She drops the book back onto her knee. “I hate her. She hates everybody.”
“She doesn’t hate everybody,” Jack says. “She’s Catholic. It’s different.”
“How is it different?”
“We hate everybody and then we feel terrible about it.”
That gets him a look instead of a laugh, quick and sideways, like the furniture just talked back. “You’ve read it,” she says.
“A couple of times.”
“Everybody’s read it. Have you *read* it?”
“‘The grandmother didn’t want to go to Florida.’”
She narrows her eyes. “The cat.”
“Pitty Sing. In a basket, under her bag, so Bailey wouldn’t find out.”
“The monkey.”
“Red Sammy’s. Chained to a chinaberry tree, picking fleas off himself like they were a delicacy.”
“Okay, *nerd*,” she says, satisfied, and uncaps the Sharpie, and turns the margin toward him so he can see what he’s up against.

body.title: “A Good Man Is Hard to Find” — the margins
body.text:
beside the grandmother, four times, bigger each time: LIAR
beside the Misfit: only honest man in it
at “Why you’re one of my babies. You’re one of my own children!” — LAST CARD. SHE’S BEGGING. PLAY IT AS A CON.

body: It’s wrong, every word of it, top to bottom, and he can’t stop reading it. She has been picking a fight with a dead woman from Milledgeville in a house full of people, and so far she’s winning.

“She’s a liar,” she says, and starts counting on the highlighters. “Page one, she doesn’t want to go to Florida, so she waves the newspaper at Bailey — escaped convict, headed this way — to scare him out of it. She sneaks the cat into the car in a basket because she knows they’d say no. And then this.” For a second she’s the grandmother herself, right there on the cushion — a little old lady in a hat, chin tucked, eyes gone enormous, fingers fluttering at her collar: “There was a *secret panel* in that house, children,” in a Georgia so sweet it could rot a tooth. Then she’s back. “Made it up. Just so the kids would scream till Bailey turned down the dirt road. And she dresses for the drive — this is my favorite —” She finds it with the yellow. “Navy straw sailor hat, white violets on the brim, so in case of an accident, anybody who sees her dead on the highway will know she was a lady.” She looks up at him again. “She’s a performer. I know performers. That last line is her best performance.”

choices.text: “She lies for twenty pages. The last thing she says is the only thing that doesn’t help her.”
response: “She lies for twenty pages,” Jack says. “Fine. Every word of it. But there’s a gun on her by the end, and she’s been flattering him for three pages to get out of it — nice people, good blood, all that. Then she says the last thing, and it’s the only thing in the story that doesn’t help her. It gets her shot.”

She points the Sharpie at him. “Ooh. Okay.” She pulls her bare feet in under her to make more room on the cushion, as though the argument needs a seat of its own. “Say more. Say it slower. I want to see if it holds.”

choices.text: “If that’s a performance, she’s not getting a callback.”
response: “If that’s a performance,” Jack says, “she’s not getting a callback.”
She laughs, straight out, nothing held back. “No,” she says. “No, she is *not*. They went with somebody younger.” She wipes under one eye with a knuckle. “Okay. Okay, you’re allowed to stay.”

choices.text: “She’s a liar. Most of the way down.”
response: “She’s a liar,” Jack says. “Most of the way down.”

“Most.” She tries it out three ways — *most*, *MOST*, *most?* — the way he has heard people run a line in a hallway before an audition, and settles on the last one. “You’re saving the bottom.” She taps the bottom of the page with the yellow, where the ditch is. “I can tell. You’ve got a face like you’re saving something.”

choices.text: “That’s the joke. Grace doesn’t wait till you’re good. It comes for a silly old woman in a ditch.”
response: “That’s the joke,” Jack says. “Grace doesn’t wait till you’re good. It comes for a silly old woman in a ditch with her hat brim broken.”
“*Grace!*” She’s a game-show host now, cards in one hand, every tooth she owns. “For four hundred.” Then she puts the cards down, and it’s only her. “Okay. Grace.”

s18.slug: SATURDAY · 12:12 AM · THE HALLORAN HOUSE, THE DEN, THE WINDOW SEAT
body: By twelve past midnight the sectional is down to three, and somebody has changed the silent channel to a cooking show. Jack’s boots are on the carpet beside hers. He doesn’t remember taking them off. Her feet are tucked under her on the cushion, close enough to his knee that he knows exactly where they are without looking, and he isn’t looking, and he knows.

body.text: She wants to know how a boy at a party in Montecito knows so much about a dead lady from Georgia. “I’ve read it,” Jack says. “And a friend of mine went as her for Halloween. With a stuffed peacock.” “What did your friend say about her?” “‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’” She says it back to herself — *I came as her. I never said she was right* — not doing anybody this time, just trying the line in her own mouth, and puts it somewhere for later.

body: “Who’s the preacher’s daughter?” Jack says. “In your movie.”

“Seventeen. Her daddy has a tent. She falls for a boy who steals out of the collection plate, and in the last scene she forgives him in the rain.” Now she’s the director, a man wearing a scarf indoors, making a frame of his fingers and looking at Jack through it. “Very O’Connor. Very *grace*.”
“In O’Connor, a bull would get him.”
“That’s what *I* said.” She points all three highlighters at him at once. “They said test audiences.”
He has been funny for twenty minutes without trying to be, and he couldn’t say when that last happened.

A guy in a visor comes down for the bar fridge, takes a beer, and stops to ask if anybody’s using the window seat. She answers him without looking up, in a long, furious, musical Swedish that may or may not be Swedish, and he takes his beer back upstairs.

Then she turns the paperback over to the end, and she is the Misfit. She hardly does anything. Her shoulders go down; her face goes courteous and patient; her voice drops into a slow Georgia drawl with nothing in it at all. Jack has seen men like that at the bus station downtown, waiting on a bus that isn’t theirs.
“No pleasure but meanness.”
Something cold goes down the back of Jack’s neck, and it isn’t the glass.

She keeps the Misfit on him for one breath more, and then she’s back, leaning in. “Here’s the thing, though. He says if Jesus raised the dead, you drop everything and follow him. And if he didn’t, you enjoy your few minutes — kill somebody, burn a house, whatever’s fun.” She taps the page with the highlighter. “That’s the most honest thing anybody says in the book. Everybody else is lying about who they are. He’s the only one who did the math.”
“How do you do that?” Jack says.
“Do what?”
“Be him.”
“I listen to how people breathe.” She says it like it’s spelling. “Everybody breathes like what they want.”
“What do I breathe like?”
She doesn’t even have to look. “Like you’re about to apologize for something.”
Jack goes back to the Misfit, where it’s safer.

She looks at him like he has said something in a language she took in high school and just remembered she can read. “Huh,” she says. “Okay. Write that down for me.” She holds out the Sharpie, and he writes TRAGEDY in her margin over the Misfit, in his small square capitals, and she blows on it to dry it.

She clutches the paperback to her chest like he’s shot her with it. “*Ow*.” Then she grins at him over the top of it, and it isn’t any of the grins from earlier: wider, a little crooked, and very interested.
