body: She gives him the Misfit once more, because she can’t leave it alone — the low shoulders, the good manners, the flat Georgia vowels of a man standing over a woman in a ditch. “She would of been a good woman, if it had been somebody there to shoot her every minute of her life.”
“Okay, Misfit,” Jack says.

She makes a face at that, a big one, for the back row. He looks out at the canyon, where there’s nothing to see but a single porch light on the far ridge, and when he looks back she has written it on the inside of the front cover — MISFIT — and drawn a box around it.
“You actually believe it,” she says. “The grace thing. You’re not just arguing.”
“I actually believe it.”
“Like a thing that happens to people.”
“Like a thing that happened to me once.”
She waits to see if there’s more. There isn’t, and she lets there not be. She only nods, slowly, and looks at him like he’s turned out taller sitting down.
“Do her line,” she says. “The last one. If it’s not a con, show me how it goes. Like you mean it.”
“I don’t do voices.”
“Everybody does voices.”
“I do one.” He touches his own chest with two knuckles. “This one.”
She looks at him for a second like he’s told her he doesn’t own shoes.

She reaches past him and slides open the glass panel at the end of the window seat. There’s a strip of deck out there, a steel rail, and after the rail nothing at all, and the November air comes in off the canyon smelling of sage and somebody’s chimney. She puts her bare feet out into it and flexes her toes at the cold like it’s a swimming pool she’s deciding about.

Then she pulls her knees back in and wraps her arms round them, and the librarian and the director and the Georgia all go out of her at once. “Okay. Real question.” This one she seems to need the answer to. “Every line, somebody wants something. That’s the job. You find the want, you play the want.” She turns the book on her knees so he can see the place — the ditch, the gun, the old woman’s hand going out. “So when she reaches out and touches him. What does she *want*?” She lets the book close on her thumb. “Because I have to forgive a boy in the rain in a month, and I don’t know what that girl wants either, and if I don’t know what she wants I can’t play her.”

response: “Nothing,” Jack says. “That’s the point. For one second she doesn’t want anything from anybody. That’s what grace looks like from the outside. And he can’t stand it.”

She doesn’t say anything. She looks down at the page, at the hand on the shoulder, and then out at the black glass, where the two of them hang over the canyon with the lamps of the den behind them, and doesn’t move, her chin on her knees, not being anybody at all.

response: “O’Connor said it herself,” Jack says. “In one of her essays. That gesture, right there, is where the grace comes in. The author’s on my side.”
“You can’t use the *author*.” She’s scandalized. “That’s cheating. That’s calling the playwright’s mother.”
“She’d want me to.”
“She’d want *everybody* shot.”

choices.text: “She wants to get to Tennessee.”
response: “She wants to get to Tennessee,” Jack says.
She throws a highlighter at him. It bounces off Theo’s shirt and rolls under the window seat, and she points after it, outraged, like it was his idea.

response: “I don’t know,” Jack says. “I just know it isn’t a con.”
She rests her chin on her knees and watches him say it. “That isn’t an answer.”
“I know.”
“It’s kind of a good one, though,” she says, and sounds annoyed about it.

body: Upstairs the music changes songs without stopping. On the sectional somebody has fallen asleep sitting up, his chin on his chest, the remote still in his hand. She fans the highlighters into the pocket of the flannel like pens in a doctor’s coat, folds her legs under her, and turns on the cushion to face him properly, with the book shut on one finger.
“Intermission,” she says. She tips her head at the sectional without looking at it. “Go on. Pick one.”
“The guy in the Lakers jersey.”

“Wants the girl on his left to notice he isn’t looking at her. She’s noticed. She’s letting him suffer, because he called her by her roommate’s name in October.” She reads them off like a menu. “The one asleep wants to go home, and his ride is upstairs doing a keg stand. The couple on the end broke up an hour ago and haven’t told each other yet.”
“You can’t know that.”
“Watch her hands.”

He watches. On the end of the sectional the girl takes her hand back out of the boy’s, carefully, a finger at a time, and folds it in her own lap, and the boy keeps watching the score as if he hadn’t felt it go.
“How do you *know* that?”
“They tell you,” she says. “Everybody’s telling you all the time. You just have to shut up long enough to hear it.” She considers that. “I’m very bad at the shutting-up part. I make up for it.”

body: “So,” she says. “Who are you?”
“Jack.”
“Jack what?”
“Costigan.”
She gives it back to him across a news desk — the anchor’s hair, the anchor’s concerned eyebrows, a hand on a stack of papers that isn’t there. “*Jack Costigan*, live from the window seat.”
“And you?”
“Skye.”
“Skye what?”
“Just the one.” She spreads her hands. “It’s a big one.”
“Like Cher.”
“Like Cher, but I can’t sing.”
“Costigan,” she says, trying it out. “Irish.”
“Half. The other half’s Calabrese.”
“So you’re Catholic twice.”
“Belt and suspenders.”
He has a girl’s name. Back at Delgado, Laney has thought about the method.
“Two girls passed me on the stairs coming down,” Jack says. “One of them thought you were somebody called Cassidy.”
“People get me confused with a girl.”
“What girl?”
“A nice one.”
“Do you go to Marisol?”
“Not yet.”
He waits for the rest of it. There isn’t any; she’s busy getting the cap back on a highlighter.
“So what do you do, Skye-just-the-one?”

She answers as somebody else: a dental hygienist from Tarzana, snapping gum, with a lisp she must have spent a summer on. Mostly she does molars. She has seen things, in molars. Then the hygienist is gone. “I act,” Skye says. “I’ve been working since I was eleven.”
“In what?” Jack says — and he sees her get ready for something. It’s small. Her chin comes up and her face goes pleasant and set, somebody at the end of a high dive deciding not to look down.

So he adds, “I don’t have a TV, so it won’t mean anything,” and goes back to the Misfit, because he wasn’t done with him. “The thing about the Misfit is, he’s the only one in the story who takes Jesus seriously —”

She laughs. It isn’t any of the laughs she’s been doing tonight. It comes out through her nose first, undignified, and then the rest of it after, and she doesn’t do a thing to tidy it up. Since eleven: Jack pictures a church-basement *Oliver!* and a commercial for a carpet outlet somewhere around Tarzana, and for the life of him he can’t see what’s funny. She’s still smiling about it a minute later, out of nowhere, as though it has come back to her on its own.
“What about you?” she says, when she can talk, wiping her eyes with the cuff of the flannel. “What do *you* do, Jack Costigan, live?”
“Philosophy.”
She puts a pipe in her mouth that isn’t there, takes it out again, and points the stem at him. “And what will you *do* with it?”
“Argue with strangers at parties.”
“You’re good at it,” she says. “I’d hire you.” Then her eyes go to his hip and back up. “You keep reaching for something. Back pocket. You’ve done it four times.”
He has. There’s nothing in it. Theo inspected him at the door of 412 and sent the paperback back to the desk with the Carhartt and the flannel. “I usually have a book.”
“I know. You keep checking it’s gone.”

Then she gives him the look again, the one from before, unhurried, all of her behind it. “You’ve got a dumped-somebody face,” she says. “Not a dumped face. A *dumped-somebody* face. They’re different. I’ve done both.” She touches her own shoulder with the end of the Sharpie. “It’s in here. Dumped people, theirs go up round their ears. People who did it look like they’re waiting for a bill.”
“Wednesday.”
“Was she nice?”
“She’s the nicest person I’ve ever met.”

Skye doesn’t do a face for that, or a voice. She nods, slowly, like it’s exactly the answer she was afraid of on his behalf. “Then you did it for her,” she says. “That’s the worst kind to do. You don’t even get to be the villain.”
He doesn’t have anything to put after that. She has known him for fifty minutes.
“Are you with somebody else?” She asks it with no one in front of it — not the anchor, not the host.
“No.”

“Okay.” Skye lets a second go by. Then she reaches over and pats his knee, twice, in sympathy. “You’re a terrible actor, Jack.”

s20a.slug: SATURDAY · 1:00 AM · THE HALLORAN HOUSE, THE DEN
body: At one o’clock somebody upstairs turns the music up, and the bass comes down through the ceiling and into the cushions. In the black glass beside her the den is laid out backward — the sectional, the cold fireplace, the floating stairs going up to the lit doorway at the top — and past the doorway, along the upper deck, somebody in a long coat goes by. Jack catches it at the edge of his eye, a shape in a reflection, and lets it go.
Skye turns her face toward the canyon, a fraction, away from the room. It’s quick, and it’s finished before he has decided whether it happened. Then she’s looking at him again.
“This party,” she says, “has too many people I went to middle school with.”
“You went to school with these people?”
“Some of them. On and off.” She already has her boots by the pull-tabs in one hand and the paperback in the other, and she’s on her bare feet on the carpet. “Do you want to leave?”
She asks it the way she asked the rest of it, straight out, like there’s no wrong answer and she’d like to hear his.
Theo said don’t move. Theo said don’t talk to anybody with a headshot. As far as Jack can see, she has a paperback and a pair of boots.

choices.text: “Yes. Let me text my roommate.”
response: “Yes,” Jack says. “Let me text my roommate.”

She takes him out through a door behind the bar fridge that he would never have found, and down a flight of bare concrete stairs toward the garage. He thumbs it on T9 going down, a letter at a time, the RAZR’s little screen the only light on the stairs.

She waits at the bottom while he sends it and stamps into his own boots, swinging hers by their tabs, and if she’s curious who the roommate is, it doesn’t show. Beside her, under a fitted gray cover, Wyatt Halloran’s father’s second car sits in the dark with its shape showing through, and past it the big door is already rolling up on the night. She ducks under before it’s halfway, barefoot on the cold concrete, without looking back to see if he’s coming.

response: “Yes,” Jack says.

She’s already moving. He grabs his boots off the carpet and goes after her in his socks, through a door behind the bar fridge he would never have found and down a flight of bare concrete stairs into the garage, past Wyatt Halloran’s father’s second car asleep under a fitted cover, without a word to anybody. The big door is already rolling up on the night. She ducks under it before it’s halfway, barefoot on the cold concrete, and he goes under after her with a boot in each hand.

s21.slug: SATURDAY · 1:10 AM · THE SAAB, MONTECITO → THE 101 NORTH
body: The car is parked on the shoulder below the turnaround, nose downhill, under a jacaranda that has dropped a season’s worth of seed pods on it, and the only light it gets is the blue that comes up out of Wyatt Halloran’s pool and spills over the edge of the canyon. It’s a Saab 900 convertible. It was red once — a red the sun has been working on for eighteen years, gone pink along the tops of the fenders. There’s a dent in the passenger door about the size of a hip. One taillight is out. The canvas top is folded down behind the seats, and somebody has mended a split seam in it with silver duct tape.

She drops her boots in the back and the O’Connor on the dash, where it slides into the corner of the windshield and rides there, and swings in barefoot. Jack watches her lean down and put the key in the floor between the seats, where there is no earthly reason for a key to go.
“It goes in the *floor*?”
“It’s Swedish,” she says, as if that settles it, and turns it.

The tape deck wakes up in the middle of a song — Fleetwood Mac, Stevie Nicks going soft and level over a drum that never hurries — and she doesn’t touch it. “It’s stuck. It’s been playing *Rumours* since August. I’ve made my peace.” She leaves the top down and puts the heater on full, and it roars at his shins.
“It’s November,” Jack says.
“You heat your feet and freeze your face. It’s the only way to drive in November.”
“Where are we going?”
“The ocean.”
He can see it from here, past the hedges: the Channel, black under the lights of the city. “It’s right there.”
“Not that one,” she says. “Mine. It’s up by you. An hour, the way I drive.”
Before she takes the brake off he asks the thing you ask in Youngstown before anybody drives you anywhere after midnight. “You have anything tonight?”
“I don’t drink where there are phones.” She says it like a rule of grammar, and pulls out.

Theo took these lanes up with the top down and Randy Newman on. She takes them down faster, and better: one hand low on the wheel and the bare foot doing all the thinking — brake late, turn in, back on the gas before the apex — and the little car leans into every hairpin and comes up out of it like it was the car’s idea. The cold pours over the windshield and takes his face clean off. Between the hedges Santa Barbara comes and goes below them, laid out along the water in lights. Somewhere around the fourth hairpin Jack laughs out loud, at nothing — at the cold, at the size of the sky — with one hand braced on the dash, and she laughs because he did and takes the next one faster. She never comes near the edge. He checks.

At the bottom she takes the on-ramp in third and puts them on the 101 north, empty at this hour, with her hair going everywhere. There’s a badge in the middle of the steering wheel. She catches him reading it and pats the dash.
“Swedish,” she says again. “Like a sauna. Like a very long, very sad film.”
“It’s GM.”
She looks over at him. “Excuse me.”
“GM bought half of Saab in 1990,” Jack says. “The rest in 2000. What year is this?”
“Ninety-one. My mother hates it.”
“Then it’s half GM. And GM’s trying to sell the rest of it, and nobody wants it.”
“How do you *know* that?”

So he tells her. Not the business page — the rest of it. That GM went bankrupt on the first of June and the Mahoning Valley watched it on the news like a ballgame they’d bet the house on. That there’s a plant in Lordstown, Ohio, twenty-five minutes from his house in Youngstown, a mile long, where his father put Cavaliers together for twenty-two years and then Cobalts — twenty-six years on the line, Local 1112 — and that he’s been laid off since June. She drives and listens. She listens the way she argued about the grandmother, all of her pointed at it, and when he stops she asks the next question, and then the one after that, and every one of them is the right one.
“And now?” she says. “What does he do all day, now?”

response: He tells her about Monday before last. The last check came and went, and his father drove down to the bar on Midlothian to watch the Steelers, who he doesn’t even like. The bar closed at two-thirty Ohio time. At one in the morning here Jack was on a stairwell in his socks with his mother on the phone, and at nine minutes to two he heard the truck take out the trash can at the curb on Glenwood Avenue. Then he heard the storm door, and his mother came back on to tell him where his father had been all night: in the employee lot at Lordstown, with the engine off. To see if the lights were on.

response: He gives her the line — the Cavaliers, the Cobalts, the union hall where somebody reads out a recall list and the name is never on it — and the garage on Glenwood Avenue: the space heater, the radio turned low, the Stroh’s fridge, the folding chair where his father listens to Ohio State now that there’s no shift to be at. How every phone call out of that garage ends the same way: *Go Bucks*, and the click.
He leaves the lot where it is, at the other end of the turnpike, with the engine off.
She drives and listens, and when he’s done she lets the quiet be quiet.

Her hands go heavy at the bottom of the wheel. “Lights are on,” she says, from the bottom of her chest, in Jack’s own vowels flattened by another thirty years of Ohio. body: It isn’t an impression. Gina does their father at the supper table sometimes, all eyebrows and grievance, and it’s funny. This isn’t funny. She has never heard Frank Costigan’s voice in her life; she has twenty minutes of Jack talking in a convertible, and out of that she has built the one thing he can’t stand to hear from anybody but the man himself — the stop before the second sentence, the weight a sentence has when it’s the only one coming. The back of Jack’s neck goes cold, and the wind has nothing to do with it.
And then she drops it. All of it — the chin, the shoulders, the vowels. What’s left is a girl driving a car with both hands, and she says it short, to the road:
“Nobody’s ever told me about their dad without wanting me to *do* something with it.”

She doesn’t explain. Jack watches the road: the white line coming at them out of the dark, the rail line running beside it, the ocean black to the edge of the world. He gives her the next thirty miles and asks her for nothing in them. She takes the Marisol exit, and Ocean Road carries them west through the sleeping town: the campus going by on the left with three windows lit in it, the eucalyptus at the Lagoon standing up black against the stars and then gone behind them.

Past the last of the campus Ocean Road gives up being Ocean Road and turns into the old coast highway, two lanes and no lights. At the stop sign where it changes she comes to a full and ostentatious stop, looks left and right at a road with nobody on it for miles, and leans out over her door to ask the dark, “Anybody?” Nobody. She’s back. She takes off with the tape rolling into the next song and tells him he looked very handsome back there, worrying about her driving, like a dad in a minivan commercial. Jack is thinking that his father would like her, and would never say so as long as he lived.

s22.slug: SATURDAY · 2:20 AM · ELLERY BEACH, THE OLD OIL-PIER PILINGS
body: Ellery Beach smells of tar and black sage and kelp gone cold on the sand. There’s no sign for it — a dirt turnout four miles up the coast from the Lagoon, a gap in a wire fence, a surfers’ path going down through the coyote brush — and at the bottom, standing out into the surf in two crooked rows, the black stumps of a pier somebody built in the twenties to pump oil out of the sea. Farther out, on the horizon, the platforms are lit up like a town that decided to stay at sea. There’s no moon. There are more stars over the water than Youngstown has ever had.
His phone goes off in his pocket as he gets out of the car.

body: He puts it away. By the time he has his door shut she’s already gone — down the path barefoot in the dark with the flannel flying open behind her — and by the time he gets to the bottom she’s in the water to her knees in her cutoffs and her black tights. A wave comes in and takes her to the thigh. She gasps like she’s been slapped, and then she laughs, and turns around in the dark with her arms out wide to show him the size of it.
“Come in,” she calls.
“It’s November.”
“It’s fifty-seven degrees. That’s warmer than the air. I checked.” She backs up a step, deeper, and the hem of the flannel goes dark. “I dare you. In your clothes.”
“Why in my clothes?”
“Because anybody can do it in their underwear.” Another step back. The sea is at her waist now, and she isn’t shivering yet, or she’s acting like she isn’t. “Clothes is a commitment, Jack.”

body: For a few minutes there’s only the shaking. His jaw has its own ideas; her teeth are going like a sewing machine, and she laughs at them, and that makes it worse. The blanket isn’t big enough for two people trying to keep any distance, so they’ve given up trying. Her shoulder is against his arm. Her hair is a wet weight that smells of the sea, and some of it is on him. The platforms burn on the horizon, smeared gold through the salt in his eyelashes.
“You stopped being sad,” she says, when her teeth let her. “About ten minutes ago. In the water.”
“Did I?”
“I was watching. It was the first thing I was going to check.”
Then she turns in the blanket and looks at him.

He’s been looked at all night — across the den, across a gearshift, across the water — but not like this. She isn’t looking at what he might say next, or at whatever he walked into that house carrying, or at where he’d rather be. She’s looking at him: here, wet, shaking, on a beach in the middle of the night, now. There isn’t anything else she’s looking at.
“I’d like to kiss you now,” she says.

In eighteen years he has never had it said to him straight out — in a sentence, with a subject and a verb. She isn’t asking whether she’s allowed to want it; that part she’s already settled, by herself, without any apology at all. She’s only asking him. His heart is going harder than the cold can account for.
He hasn’t moved. So she starts on the next sentence, easy, leaving him a door — “You can tell me —”

s23a.slug: SATURDAY · 3:15 AM · THE SAAB, THE WINDOWS FOGGED
body: He’s the one. He gets an elbow under himself and comes up out from under her hair, and the cold rushes in everywhere she was.
“That’s —” he says. “I should —”
He doesn’t know the end of either sentence. She sits back on her heels in the blanket and looks at him, wet and interested. He looks for hurt in her face, and it isn’t there.
“Huh,” she says.
He waits for the bit. There isn’t one.
“You stop,” she says. “Okay.” She says it like a note she’s making in a margin, to come back to. Then: “Car. I can’t feel my *legs*.”

In the Saab with the top up and the heater roaring at their shins, their clothes start to steam. The windows fog from the bottom up until the platforms are a gold smear and then not even that, and the tape turns itself over every forty minutes or so and starts the side again, so that the same song comes around, and comes around, until it stops being a song and turns into the weather.

And they talk. She takes Youngstown off him a piece at a time — Nonna’s gravy, the snow that’s gray by noon, Gina who texts in lowercase, Rosie who mails him crabs — and he gets Studio City, which is, she says, “an apartment my mother rented for the commute,” and nothing more. She tells him the worst callback she ever had — twelve years old, a juice commercial, falling in love with a juice box in front of eleven men eating sandwiches — and does all eleven men. He tells her the best paperback he ever found for two dollars, a *Moviegoer* off a church rummage table with a stranger’s fights with Walker Percy running down every margin in green ink. She wants to know who won. The margins, mostly, he tells her, and she says that’s how it ought to be.
It goes on for two and a half hours. Afterward he won’t be able to say what most of it was about.
Then the glass starts to change. A gray comes up behind the fog, and he only notices it because her face has begun to come out of the dark beside him a little at a time, freckles first.

s23b.slug: SATURDAY · 3:15 AM · ELLERY BEACH, THE SAAB, TOP DOWN
body: He doesn’t stop. She does.

She lifts her head, and he sees it arrive before she opens her mouth: the chin tucks, the eyebrows go up under the brim of a hat that isn’t there, and she is the grandmother — Georgia to the bone, a navy straw sailor with white violets on it.
“That’s enough for a first night,” she says. “In case of an accident, everyone should know I’m a lady.”
He laughs so hard he gets sand in his mouth.
Then she’s herself again, grinning down at him, out of breath. “Car,” she says. “I can’t feel my *legs*.”

She puts the top down. It’s the only way to drive in November, she reminds him, and they aren’t driving, but the rule stands: heater on full, the blanket pulled over both of them up to the chin, the canvas folded back, and every star over the Pacific right there overhead.

And they talk. She gets Youngstown out of him a piece at a time — the snow that’s gray by noon, Nonna’s gravy, Gina who texts in lowercase, Rosie who mails him crabs — and he gets Studio City, which is “an apartment my mother rented for the commute,” and nothing more. She tells him the worst callback she ever had: twelve years old, a juice commercial, falling in love with a juice box in front of eleven men eating sandwiches. She does all eleven men. He tells her about the best paperback he ever found for two dollars, a *Moviegoer* off a church rummage table with a stranger’s fights with Walker Percy down every margin in green ink, and she wants to know who won. The margins, mostly, he says. She says that’s how it ought to be.
It goes on for two and a half hours. The tape in the deck turns itself over every forty minutes or so, and the same song keeps coming around under the stars.

Somewhere near the end of it the stars over the water start thinning from the east, and the sky lets go of the sea along a line of gray at the bottom of everything, where an hour ago there wasn’t any line at all.

s23k.slug: SATURDAY · 3:03 AM · ELLERY BEACH, THE SAND
body: Her mouth tastes of salt. That’s the first thing — salt, and cold, and then not cold, because she’s warm inside it and she isn’t careful about anything. Her hands come up out of the blanket and find the back of his neck, and they’re freezing, both of them, two shocks right where his hair is wet; and then they aren’t, because she leaves them there and his neck warms them, and somehow the warming is the part that undoes him.

He gets a hand into her hair. There’s so much of it — heavy and wet, full of the sea and a little sand, cold at the ends and warm at the roots — and she makes a sound against his mouth when he does, low and pleased, and comes closer, and the blanket slides off one of his shoulders and lets the night in down his back. He doesn’t care. The wet flannel under his other hand is cold, and she isn’t, under it.

She kisses him the way she’s done everything else tonight, as though it’s the only thing happening anywhere and she has decided to be there for it. She doesn’t hurry. Once she laughs, right against his mouth, at something — at them, at the cold, at his jaw still going — and the laugh goes straight through him, and she kisses him again with the laugh still in it.
Once she pulls back just far enough to see him, and looks, as if checking he’s still the same person, and says, “Hi,” and he says, “Hi,” and she comes back while he’s still saying it.

His body has no opinion about any of this except *more*. He’s eighteen and freezing and has been single since Wednesday and has spent two days carrying something he wouldn’t name to anybody, and all of that is somewhere up the beach with her boots. There’s only this: her cold nose against his cheek and her warm mouth, the sand working into everything, the wet denim, the weight of her leaning in. He wants this. He isn’t going to lie to himself that he doesn’t.

Something in him that has sat very still all fall, with its hands folded, gets up. She catches his lower lip between hers and lets it go, and he hears himself laugh, low, and doesn’t recognize the sound, and kisses her harder for it, and she lets him, and gives it back.

Under it — not a voice, nothing like a sermon — is one simple physical fact he keeps coming back to: he is exactly here. Ellery Beach, three in the morning, four miles up the coast from everything he knows, kissing a girl whose last name he doesn’t have, whose hands he could pick out of a crowd now and whose house he couldn’t find with a map. It is very strange, and it isn’t strange at all, and he keeps kissing her through both.

At some point they go over sideways into the sand, still tangled in the blanket, and she ends up half on top of him, up on one elbow, her hair coming down around both their faces like a tent with the stars at its edges. She kisses him from there for a little while. Slower. Then not slower.

The tide has turned somewhere without telling them. A wave runs farther up the sand than the others and finds the bottom of his jeans, and the cold of it goes up his leg and straight through him. She lifts her head. Her mouth is right there. Her eyes are right there, and so is everything in them.
One of them is going to have to stop. It’s a fact about tonight, like the tide.

body: In the first of the gray she gets out of the car without a word and goes back down the path to the water, and he goes after her, because apparently that is what he does now. She walks in to the waist in the flannel, and so does he, and it’s worse the second time. “That’s how you know you meant the first one,” she says, through her teeth. Then they run for the car, and she turns the heater as far as it goes.

She drives him back down the coast with the top up and nobody talking. It’s new for both of them, and he isn’t going to be the one to spoil it. The old highway turns back into Ocean Road. The campus comes up out of the dark on the right, every window black. St. Brendan’s goes by across the road, the A-frame and its blue glass still holding the night, and he looks at it, and then at the road again.
At the light by the Anacapa turn she yawns for the first time all night, hugely, without covering it. “I have a thing at nine,” she says. “In a different county.” She doesn’t say what the thing is.

The Anacapa lot at ten to six: the sodium lights still buzzing on their poles and going pale, a sky over the hills that has started to have a color without deciding which one, the eucalyptus along the Lagoon black against it. Delgado is dark from top to bottom except for one window on the fourth floor.

He’s soaked again to the ribs. His jeans are as heavy as a pair of waders, Theo’s shirt is stuck to his back with the salt crusting at the cuffs, and there’s sand in places he’d rather not think about, and he can’t stop grinning, and he’s given up trying.
She puts it in park and leaves the engine running. The tape has come around to the same song again.
“Will I —” he starts.
“Yes,” she says. “Obviously. Don’t be a dad about it.” She holds out her hand. “Phone.”
He gives her the RAZR. She flips it open, finds the contacts on the second try, starts typing, stops, and stares at the screen.
“It’s *guessing*,” she says, outraged. “I didn’t ask it to guess.”
“It’s T9.”
“It’s a *liar*.” She finds the setting that makes it stop helping and does it the long way, letter by letter, swearing at the 9, and turns the little screen around to show him: SKYE (MISFIT).

Then she presses call. In the pocket of her flannel a phone lights up white through the damp cotton and starts to buzz. She takes it out — an iPhone, white, his number across the screen — and reads it, satisfied.
“Three-three-oh,” she says. “Ohio. Now I have you.”
“What’s your last name?”
“Out.”
She leans across him — salt, wet hair, warm — and opens his door.

Then he’s standing in the lot with the door shut and the Saab already moving, one taillight, the tape still going, and the sound of it gets smaller down the road toward Las Olas until there’s nothing in the road at all but the gulls coming in off the Lagoon.
He turns around. Theo’s SL is in its space, nose out, the top up, dew on the hood.

Theo lies back down in his coat and shuts his eyes. He may even be asleep.

s26.slug: SATURDAY · 9:00 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: On the Fishbowl TV the blimp hangs over Ann Arbor, and the Big House is maize and blue to the rim except for one loud scarlet corner. Nine in the morning here is noon there. The Fishbowl has a boy asleep on the far couch under a Marisol Surf hoodie, a girl at the window counter eating dry cereal out of the box, and Jack, on the near couch, who hasn’t been to bed.

He’s talking to the set. He doesn’t try not to. Pryor keeps it on third down with half of Michigan hanging off him, and Jack says, “*There* it is.” Michigan’s freshman throws one straight to a scarlet jersey, and Jack says, “Thank you, Tate,” and means it. When the camera finds Tressel on the sideline in the sweater vest with his arms folded, Jack tells him, “Don’t smile. You’ll pull something.” In the garage on Glenwood his father would grunt at the good parts. Here the girl with the cereal box looks over once and decides to allow it.

It’s the game Becca put in her planner, in green. At the far end of the couch, in his navy silk robe, Theo Vance is watching Jack instead of it, with the expression he usually saves for subtitled films at the point where everybody’s motives get complicated.
At a commercial he asks, “Which ones are we?”
“Red.”
“Scarlet. I can see it’s scarlet. I mean *why*. What did Michigan ever do to you?”

Jack tells him. Woody Hayes, who wouldn’t say the word and called it *that school up north*, and who supposedly ran low on gas one night just short of Ohio and pushed his car over the line rather than buy a gallon in Michigan; Bo; the ten years of Woody and Bo; John Cooper, who lost to them ten times in thirteen tries and whose name his father still won’t allow in the house. It takes most of the commercials in the first quarter.
“So it’s a vendetta,” Theo says. “With a band.”

Laney turns up at the end of the first quarter in sweatpants and full makeup, with a Diet Coke, and folds her forearms on the back of the couch behind Theo, and they confer. Jack, watching Michigan go three-and-out, gets pieces of it.
“—why is he *humming*—”
“I don’t *know*. He came in *wet*. I lost him for seven hours—”
“You *lost* him?”
“There was a heron—”

Ohio State runs it up the middle for twelve yards and Jack says, “There you go,” and the conference breaks up. Laney leans over the couch back with the bright interest of a judge at the interview round.

body.text: “Theodore tells me you *walked* home. From *Montecito*.” “Most of it’s downhill,” Jack says.
“Theodore tells me you talked about a *book* all night.” “A short story,” Jack says. “It’s short.”
“Theodore tells me you won’t say where you went.” “He won’t say where he went either,” Jack says, and Theo, at the end of the couch, says, “I was *looking for you*,” with real feeling.

body: Laney lets that one go and tries another. “Jack. How’s Becca?”
“She’s okay,” Jack says, watching the snap. “She flies home Wednesday.”
Laney looks at Theo as if he were personally responsible. Then she plays her last card. “Lena’s still sick. She sounds like a *foghorn*.”
“Tell her to eat the soup,” Jack says. He means it, and he says it to the television, and Michigan snaps the ball.
Laney straightens up off the couch very slowly and goes to sit somewhere she can see his face.

Then Michigan gives it away again, and Jack is up off the couch with both arms over his head before the officials have sorted out the pile, and the boy under the Marisol Surf hoodie lifts his head, takes in the situation, and puts it back down. Laney, who regards football as something that happens to other girls’ boyfriends, comes around and sits on the arm of the couch to see what the noise is about. Theo asks what a safety is. Jack explains it twice, with the remote, and Theo says it sounds like a tax.
At halftime ABC goes back to the studio. Jack mutes a man in a suit standing in front of a wall of numbers and turns sideways on the couch, and he doesn’t build up to it.

body.text: The last time he had this sentence in his mouth, walking home at one in the morning, it turned into a joke about Lupe’s on the way out. This one comes out straight.

body: “Come to Youngstown for Thanks—”
“Yes,” says Theo.
“I didn’t finish.”
“Why? Yes.” Theo sits up and straightens his robe, an ambassador presenting credentials. “I’ll bring a hostess gift. What do you people drink — Folgers?”
“It’s the Greyhound. Two and a half days.”
“The *bus*.” Theo looks at the muted studio and visibly reconsiders nothing. “Is there a dining car?”
Behind him Laney has set her Diet Coke down on the back of the couch. “Theodore Vance,” she says, “on a *Greyhound*. I would pay money. I would pay my *daddy’s* money.”
“I’ve been on a bus,” Theo says, with dignity. “In Prague. It was an art project.”

body.text: Theo takes the Residential Services receipt out of his robe pocket — he carries it now — and writes under the jar, on his knee: + 1 THANKSGIVING (YOUNGSTOWN). PAYABLE IN PIE.

s27.slug: SATURDAY · 12:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: Ohio State 21, Michigan 10. Two hundred and fifty-one yards on the ground in the other team’s house, and the sixth straight. At twenty to one Jack has the RAZR out on the fourth-floor landing of the east stairwell, where the window looks east over the eucalyptus to the hills. He stands with the phone in his hand and doesn’t call anybody yet. The hills are brown and bare in the noon light, with houses here and there in the folds.

body.text: It buzzes in his hand. DAD.
“Six straight,” says Frank Costigan.
“Six straight, Pop.”
“Still Pasadena,” his father says. He seems to like the word.

Behind his father the garage radio is still on the postgame, turned low. Frank has some things to say about the running game and one thing to say about the Michigan coach, whom he has decided to pity. Then, in the same voice: “Your mother says the bus.”
“I’m bringing my roommate.”
“The rich one?”
“Yeah.”
“Huh.” There’s a pause on the line with an opinion in it, possibly two. “Your mother’ll feed him,” his father says, and the line clicks.

body: When he gets back to 412, Theo is at his desk in the robe with the MacBook open, and he turns it around without a word. On the screen is an itinerary with both their names on it: Santa Barbara to Pittsburgh, Wednesday morning, one change, two seats together.
“I was invited,” Theo says. “Guests bring something.”
“I have a bus ticket.”

“You have a voucher. You call them on Monday and tell them you’ve had a better offer. I looked into it.” Theo has had the word *bus* in his head since halftime, and it shows. “It left Monday *night*, Costigan. You’d have been in Nebraska by Wednesday, next to a man with a ham sandwich. Now you leave Wednesday, like a person.” He uncaps a pen. “What’s your address? For the flowers.”
“No flowers.”
“It’s customary. A guest sends flowers ahead. It establishes a *tone* —”
“Theo. You send lilies to Glenwood Avenue, my grandmother’s going to ask who died.”
“Glenwood,” says Theo, and writes it on the back of his hand.
For a second Jack can see it: Theo in the doorway on Glenwood with a hostess gift nobody can identify, and Nonna taking his face in both hands to find out whether he eats.
“What were you going to do? For Thanksgiving.”

“My mother’s doing it in Montecito with a man who sells crystals. My father’s doing it in Cabo with his wife. Poppy’s doing it with whichever of them loses.” Theo caps the pen. “I had a reservation somewhere. I’ll cancel it. I’m getting good at that.”

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name. A week to the night, I asked about the table. She’ll be okay. Julian says call him from the bathroom. I didn’t ask the other thing. Becca’s done. It’s me and the Greyhound. Theo’s coming. I asked him at halftime of Michigan; he said yes before I finished. Two seats to Pittsburgh, Wednesday. The Greyhound’s a voucher.

s28.slug: SATURDAY · 5:45 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 → THE 4TH-FLOOR HALL
body: It has been dark for an hour. The charcoal shirt is back on its hanger on Theo’s closet door, dried stiff, with the salt still on the cuffs, and Theo has looked at the cuffs twice today and kept his opinion to himself. Jack is in his Anchor shirt for the seven o’clock, sitting on the edge of his bed to tie his shoes, and Theo is lying on his own bed with his iPhone to his ear, talking to Laney as though Jack were a lamp.
“—I don’t *know*, Delaney. He’s *happy*.” A pause. “No. *No* girls. I checked every room. Twice.” A longer pause. “Because I *would* have seen.”
He hangs up and looks across at Jack. Jack finishes the second knot and stands.
“Night, Theo.”
“Costigan.”
Jack stops at the door. Theo is looking at him from the pillow with the phone still in his hand, and for a second there’s a short question on his face.
“Bring me fries,” Theo says.

Out in the hall the fourth floor is getting ready to go out: a hair dryer behind 418, “Bad Romance” through somebody’s door, two guys at the bathroom mirror arguing about whether a hoodie counts as a jacket. Jack takes the RAZR out and opens it, and the contacts fall open at S, where she put herself: SKYE (MISFIT). He starts a new message. He types *misfit* the old way, a letter at a time — the 6, the 4 three times, the 7 four times for the *s* — and looks at it on the little screen, and takes it back out the same way, one letter at a time.

He shuts the phone. Down at the end of the hall Doug’s door is open, and the blue of somebody’s raid is moving on his ceiling. Jack puts the RAZR in his pocket and keeps his hand on it, and goes to work.
